Multiple sclerosis (MS)

A double-blind crossover publication reported improved force recovery at one dose and greater muscle strength in a second experiment, while muscle fatigue did not improve. Another small study reported increased IL-10 but no change in nitrite levels.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A double-blind crossover publication reported improved force recovery at one dose and greater muscle strength in a second experiment, while muscle fatigue did not improve. Another small study reported increased IL-10 but no change in nitrite levels.

Summary of the Evidence

The multiple-sclerosis category contains 18 unique titles: five human reports, five mouse studies, two in-vitro or ex-vivo reports, three narrative reviews, two systematic reviews and one protocol. Human evidence includes two randomized reports and three other studies. The key 2024 crossover publication contains two experiments with 31 and 23 participants; it is one paper, not two publications or a large independent trial. The reviews summarize primary reports.

Human and clinical evidence

Rouhani et al. tested PBM in two double-blind crossover experiments in people with MS. The first found better force recovery at a higher dose than placebo, while muscle fatigue did not improve. The second found greater muscle strength after active PBM than after placebo (Rouhani et al. 2024). A separate small clinical study reported increased IL-10 after PBM but no change in nitrite levels; these are immune markers, not evidence of reduced relapse or disability. Another pilot applying light under the tongue or over the radial artery reported no effect on fatigue. Older comparison reports include co-interventions and limited control of expectancy.

Animal evidence

Five mouse publications examine experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis or related demyelination models. A systematic review of three controlled animal studies reported reduced clinical severity and inflammatory or myelin-related measures, while noting high risk of bias in the underlying work (Ahmer et al. 2024). These findings are preclinical.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Two laboratory publications examine immune or blood-cell responses. They provide mechanistic data rather than clinical outcomes.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Human studies use near-infrared light, including an 808-nm schedule in the fatigue and immune-marker reports. The 2024 muscle-function study used several dose levels, including 40, 80 and 120 J, but the database does not provide one wavelength and treatment schedule common to all trials. Routes include transcranial, sublingual and radial-artery application. These target tissues and outcomes differ substantially.

Interpretation

The evidence supports a possible acute effect on selected muscle-force measures. It does not show that PBM reduces fatigue consistently, changes MS disability or modifies inflammatory disease activity. Small samples, different target routes and surrogate outcomes limit the clinical meaning of the current findings.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term strength outcomes in people with mild-to-moderate MS Very low for fatigue, daily function, or disease activity
Publications and records18 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The strongest human report used two small crossover experiments and found selected force or strength gains, but not lower muscle fatigue. Other clinical reports measured fatigue or immune markers and do not demonstrate disease modification. Larger independent sham-controlled studies should test everyday function, fatigue and disability over longer follow-up.
